archetype.name: Pretender (record ahead of its play)
archetype.definition: A team whose November surge and handful of overtime points make it look like it is climbing back toward last spring's playoff form, while its 5-on-5 play says it belongs near the bottom of the league.

report.headline: A 4-1 heater built on one-goal games can't hide 29th-ranked play
report.take:
The Flyers come off a 98-point season and a playoff run that produced four wins. Twenty-six games into 2026-27 they are 9-11-6, sixth in the Metropolitan, and 24th on the site. The record is the flattering part. They rank 29th in goal differential per game at -0.81, 30th in goals scored per game, and 29th in both 5-on-5 shares that describe how games are actually played: 44% of the expected goals and 46% of the shot attempts. That last part is new. In each of the previous three seasons their xGF % sat above 50%, including 0.506 last year. Whatever carried them to the playoffs at 5-on-5 has not come back.

The season splits cleanly in two. October was a disaster: 3-11, with only 2.07 goals a game, and the nine-game losing streak sits inside it. November has been a .500-plus team at 6-5, with scoring up to 3.45 a game. The last five games went 4-1-0 for an .800 points percentage, and that run is why the mood has lifted. Look at how it was won, though. Four wins, every one by a single goal, one of them 6-5 in overtime at Ottawa, against 19 goals allowed in five games. Across the last ten the differential is -2. They are scoring more, but they are not preventing anything.

The numbers hide less than the standings do. Pts vs Goal Diff is +2, ninth in the league. The six overtime losses have banked points that a -21 goal differential would not normally earn, and the franchise has run positive on that stat in every recent season. The 5-on-5 PDO of 98.3 is below average, so this is not a team riding a hot percentage that is about to crash. It is a team being out-chanced while its goaltending sits roughly at average.

The roster grades fit that picture. The forwards rate B+, led by Denver Barkey, sixth on the centers tab with 13 points and a 54% expected-goals share. The blueline is a C- and Cam York sits at -8. The goaltending is a C split exactly down the middle: Joseph Woll is slightly above expected, Dan Vladar well below. The Flyers can win shootouts and coin flips. Until the 5-on-5 share climbs back toward where it lived for three straight years, the realistic ceiling is a fringe team, not a playoff one.

strengths.title: Forward group carrying the offense
strengths.body: The forwards grade B+, the best group on the roster. Barkey is the engine: 13 points, five on the power play, and a 54% expected-goals share while every team metric around him sits below 50%. November's jump to 3.45 goals a game shows the forwards can produce. With team offense still ranked 29th over the full season, though, it is a recent trend rather than an established level.

strengths.title: Penalty kill holds the line
strengths.body: The PK runs at 77.2%, exactly the league average and 18th overall. Shots allowed are about average too, at 27.4 a game. Special-teams defense is not where the Flyers bleed. That is likely to hold, since last year's PK finished at the same 77.6% level.

strengths.title: Woll as the steadier net option
strengths.body: Woll has saved 1.9 goals above expected with a .892 save %, and he is 25th of 72 on the goalies tab. On a team losing the chance battle, a goalie who simply stops what he should is worth leaning on. He has had exactly as many starts as Vladar, which looks like the easiest lever available.

concerns.title: Out-chanced badly at 5-on-5
concerns.body: An xGF % of 0.44 and a CF % of 0.46 both rank 29th, six points below the league on expected goals. This is a break from the club's recent identity, since it sat above 50% on expected goals in each of the last three seasons. It is the core reason the goal differential is 29th. It does not depend on luck, so it will not fix itself.

concerns.title: Recent wins are coin flips
concerns.body: The 4-1-0 last five came with only a +1 differential. Every win was by one goal, and 19 goals went in against in five games. Pts vs Goal Diff already sits ninth in the league at +2. A team allowing 3.8 a game over its hot streak is not winning it on merit, and those one-goal results tend to even out.

concerns.title: Leaky blueline, split crease
concerns.body: The defense allows centers 0.22 points a game above their expected output, the worst mark in the league, and ranks 29th against all forwards. The C- blueline and York's -8 fit that. Vladar's -3.9 GSAx across half the starts drags the combined save % down to .885. The power play doesn't offset any of it: at 18.1% it ranks 28th, well under the league's 22.5%.

trend.note: October's 3-11 hole gave way to a 6-5 November and a 4-1-0 last five, with scoring up sharply. The defense has not improved at all over that stretch, so the climb rests on goals for and one-goal finishes.

weekAhead.headline: Three soft defenses, one Islanders wall: a chance to bank points
weekAhead.body:
Three of the four opponents can't keep the puck out. Washington's goaltending grades F with a .869 save %, Vancouver is last on the site with the league's worst goal differential, and Toronto sits 27th on the site with defense ranked 27th. That suits a Flyers team whose recent wins came by outscoring people. The catch is in Washington, where the Capitals own 53.5% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, and the Flyers' 44% share means they should expect to spend long stretches defending.

The Islanders game on the 28th is the outlier. New York is ninth on the site, with goalies second in the league at +13.4 GSAx and a defense that holds centers well under their averages. Toronto's power play, sixth in the league, also tests a PK that is only average. Three wins in four is plausible. Anything less than five standings points from this week would be a missed opportunity.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs Vancouver's sieve PK
keyMatchups.body: Vancouver kills only 61.2% of penalties, 31st in the league, and its goalies are 11.7 goals below expected, worst in the league. The Flyers' 28th-ranked power play will not find a better spot to get going. The Canucks also allow wingers 0.37 points a game above expected.

keyMatchups.title: Capitals' shot pressure vs a shaky blueline
keyMatchups.body: Washington ranks ninth in offense and sixth in xGF %, so the Flyers will be out-chanced. The Capitals' .869 save % is the opening. This sets up as a high-event game the Flyers can win only by finishing their chances.

keyMatchups.title: Islanders goaltending and center coverage
keyMatchups.body: New York's goalies are second in GSAx and its defense ranks fifth at containing centers. That cuts straight at Barkey, the Flyers' best producer. Expect a low-scoring game where their 0-for-the-chance-battle tendency gets exposed.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the defense can hold anyone under three goals; the scoring is there, but 3.8 allowed a game over the hot streak is not a sustainable way to win.

restOfSeason.body:
At this pace the Flyers finish around 76 points. That is the same total as their 2024-25 season and well short of last year's 98. November's scoring jump is the most encouraging sign, and the forward group and Barkey suggest it is partly real. Offense in the 2.8-3.2 range the rest of the way is reasonable. What is not real is the run of one-goal wins: with a 5-on-5 share near the league's bottom and goals against running high, the close-game edge should fade.

The path to the playoff mix runs through the crease and the blueline, not the forwards. Riding Woll more heavily would help, and so would an xGF % that drifts back toward the 50% level of the past three seasons. Absent that, expect a team that hovers a little below .500 in points percentage and finishes in the bottom third of the conference.

swingFactors: 5-on-5 shot share returning toward recent seasons
Woll taking the bulk of the starts
Power play climbing out of the bottom five

confidence.note: 26 games, and the bad 5-on-5 numbers are consistent all season, but the roster sheet lists only a handful of players and the all-situations finishing figures look thin.
